'''Lyman Alexander Page, Jr.''' (born September 24, 1957) is the [[James Smith McDonnell|James S. McDonnell]] Distinguished University Professor of [[Physics]] at [[Princeton University]]. He is an expert in observational [[Physical cosmology|cosmology]] and one of the original co-investigators for the [[Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe]] (WMAP) project that made precise observations of the [[electromagnetic radiation]] from the [[Big Bang]], known as [[cosmic microwave background radiation]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Lyman Page |publisher=[[American Physical Society]] |url=https://www.aps.org/about/governance/election/page.cfm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150520154829/https://www.aps.org/about/governance/election/page.cfm |archive-date=May 20, 2015 |access-date=May 20, 2015}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Page was born in [[San Francisco]]<ref name="autobio"/> in 1957, and moved through [[Virginia]] and [[New Hampshire]] with his parents, eventually settling in [[Maine]]. His father was a [[Pediatrics|pediatrician]] and his mother an [[artist]].<ref>{{cite web |title=InterViews: Lyman Page |url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/podcasts/interviews/lyman-page.html |publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences]] |access-date=July 4, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220704063859/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/podcasts/interviews/lyman-page.html |archive-date=July 4, 2022}}</ref> He has a younger brother and sister. He became interested in [[physics]] at [[Bowdoin College]], [[Brunswick, Maine]], where he did his [[Undergraduate education|undergraduate studies]], after a course taught by Elroy O. LaCasce. He worked on the [[Mach’s principle]] for a course project and was drawn to [[Physical cosmology|cosmology]].<ref name="autobio"/> Page graduated with a [[Bachelor of Arts|BA]] in Physics in 1978.<ref name="newcv"/>

Page then became a research technician for 15 months at the [[Bartol Research Institute|Bartol Research Foundation]] (now [[Bartol Research Institute]]), being stationed at the [[McMurdo Station]] in the [[Antarctica]] and operating a [[cosmic ray]] station.<ref name="autobio"/><ref name="steppe">{{cite news |last1=Даулетбек |first1=Кайсар |title=From a sailor to the Breakthrough Prize winner: Interview with Doctor Lyman Page |url=https://the-steppe.com/steppe-english/from-a-sailor-to-the-breakthrough-prize-winner-interview-with-doctor-lyman-page |access-date=July 5, 2022 |work=the-steppe.com |date=October 12, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705015750/https://the-steppe.com/steppe-english/from-a-sailor-to-the-breakthrough-prize-winner-interview-with-doctor-lyman-page |archive-date=July 5, 2022}}</ref> Returning to the [[United States]], he bought and rebuilt a [[sailboat]], and started sailing around the [[East Coast of the United States|East Coast]] and the [[Caribbean]] for 2.5 years.<ref name="steppe"/> He intermittently worked onshore in [[carpentry]], [[rigging]] and other kinds of boat service, until he survived a storm near [[Venezuela]], after which he decided to pursue [[graduate studies]].<ref name="autobio"/> [[Rainer Weiss]] from the [[MIT Department of Physics|Department of Physics]] of the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) agreed to let Page work in his lab, albeit without pay, so Page worked as carpenter in the day and at Weiss's lab at night.<ref name="autobio"/> Eventually in 1983, Page began his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] study at the MIT under the supervision of Stephan S. Meyer, completing 6 years later.<ref name="newcv"/>

== Scientific career ==
After his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]], Page stayed at MIT as a [[postdoctoral researcher]], and joined the [[Princeton University Department of Physics|Department of Physics]] of [[Princeton University]] in 1990, first as an instructor, and then promoted to [[assistant professor]] 1 year later and [[associate professor]] in 1995.<ref name="newcv"/> He became a [[Professor|full professor]] in 1998.<ref name="newcv"/> Since 2005, he has been successively appointed to different [[Financial endowment#Endowed professorships|endowed professorships]], including the [[Henry DeWolf Smyth]] Professor of Physics (2005-2014), the [[Cyrus Fogg Brackett Chair of Physics]] (2014-2015) and the [[James Smith McDonnell|James S. McDonnell]] Distinguished University Professor of Physics (since 2015).<ref>{{cite web |title=CURRICULUM VITAE LYMAN ALEXANDER PAGE JR. |url=https://phy-page-imac.princeton.edu//~page/cv_2pg_sep15.pdf |publisher=Princeton University |access-date=July 4, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220704063709/https://phy-page-imac.princeton.edu//~page/cv_2pg_sep15.pdf |archive-date=July 4, 2022 |date=September 2015}}</ref>

Between 2011 and 2017, Page was the chair, or Head, of the Department of Physics of Princeton University.<ref name="newcv"/>

Page was the founding director of the [[Atacama Cosmology Telescope]] project from 2004 to 2014.<ref>{{cite news |title=New view of nature's oldest light adds fresh twist to debate over universe's age |url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2020/07/15/new-view-natures-oldest-light-adds-fresh-twist-debate-over-universes-age |access-date=July 6, 2022 |publisher=Princeton University |date=July 15, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220706023743/https://www.princeton.edu/news/2020/07/15/new-view-natures-oldest-light-adds-fresh-twist-debate-over-universes-age |archive-date=July 6, 2022}}</ref> Currently, he is a member of the executive board of the [[Simons Observatory]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Executive Board |date=February 28, 2020 |url=https://simonsobservatory.org/executive-board/ |publisher=[[Simons Observatory]] |access-date=July 8, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220708022909/https://simonsobservatory.org/executive-board/ |archive-date=July 8, 2022}}</ref> an Advisor for Gravity and the Extreme Universe at the [[Canadian Institute for Advanced Research]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Lyman Page |url=https://cifar.ca/bios/lyman-page/ |publisher=[[Canadian Institute for Advanced Research]] |access-date=July 6, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705085900/https://cifar.ca/bios/lyman-page/ |archive-date=July 5, 2022}}</ref> and serves on the board of directors of the [[Research Corporation|Research Corporation for Science Advancement]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Lyman A. Page Jr., Ph.D. |url=https://rescorp.org/rcsa/about/board-of-directors/lyman-a-page-jr-ph.d |publisher=[[Research Corporation]] |access-date=July 5, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705073015/https://rescorp.org/rcsa/about/board-of-directors/lyman-a-page-jr-ph.d |archive-date=July 5, 2022}}</ref>

== Research ==
Page's research centers around the [[Cosmic microwave background]] (CMB), which is the [[electromagnetic radiation]] from the [[Big Bang]]. In 1991, Page, together with [[David Todd Wilkinson]], [[Norman Jarosik]] and Edward J. Wollack, conceived of a satellite designed to specifically detect CMB.<ref name="autobio"/> They eventually partnered with [[Johns Hopkins University]], [[University of California, Los Angeles]], the [[NASA]] [[Goddard Space Flight Center]] and other institutions,<ref>{{cite web |title=WMAP Institutions |url=https://map.gsfc.nasa.gov/mission/team.html |publisher=[[Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe]] |access-date=July 5, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705084812/https://map.gsfc.nasa.gov/mission/team.html |archive-date=July 5, 2022}}</ref> and the effort became the [[Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe]] (WMAP) project, which was named in honor of Wilkinson.<ref>{{cite web |title=Lyman A. Page Jr. |publisher=[[Princeton University Department of Physics|Department of Physics]], [[Princeton University]] |url=https://phy.princeton.edu/people/lyman-page-jr |access-date=July 5, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705072009/https://phy.princeton.edu/people/lyman-page-jr |archive-date=July 5, 2022}}</ref> The satellite was launched in 2001. Since CMB comes from a time when the [[universe]] began, WMAP enables the study of the universe's early history, including its [[Expansion of the universe|expansion]], as well as its [[Universe#Composition|composition]].<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Pearson |first=Ezzy |date=June 15, 2021 |title=WMAP: the NASA mission that mapped the cosmic microwave background |url=https://www.skyatnightmagazine.com/space-missions/wmap-cosmic-microwave-background/ |magazine=[[BBC Sky at Night]] |location=[[London]] |access-date=July 5, 2022 |archive-date=July 5, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705075656/https://www.skyatnightmagazine.com/space-missions/wmap-cosmic-microwave-background/}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Page met his wife, Elizabeth Olson, during his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] years at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. Olson is a [[biophysics]] [[professor]] at [[Columbia University]]. They have three boys.<ref name="autobio"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Elizabeth S. Olson, PhD |date=April 23, 2018 |url=https://www.entcolumbia.org/profile/eolson |publisher=[[Columbia University]] |access-date=July 5, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705014646/https://www.entcolumbia.org/profile/eolson |archive-date=July 5, 2022}}</ref>
